articles.text: In the first weekend of October, Cub Scouts and parents descended on Bort Meadows in Chabot Regional Park near Castro Valley for two nights and one day filled with activities. articles.text: On Monday, October 4, City Council determined that conducting meetings with the public attending in City Hall could present imminent risk to the health and safety of attendees. It issued a resolution proclaiming a continuing need to meet remotely. All five members of the council and City Administrator Sara Lillevand were present at the October 4 meeting, which residents were able to join virtually. The pandemic has resulted in changes to how local governments conduct business, and legislative bodies were freed from some Brown Act requirements in light of the COVID-19 public health crisis that continues to linger. Now, with vaccine availability, some legislative bodies have once again welcomed the public to in-person meetings; at the same time, state Legislature has stepped in to formally amend open meeting laws to account for a new reality. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 361 into law on September 15, which allows local legislative bodies to continue meeting by teleconference, or remotely, during a proclaimed state of emergency. The governor’s original executive order allowing for virtual meetings was set to expire on June 15, the day the statewide shutdown was set to end. Instead, Gov. Newsom announced an extension allowing local agencies to conduct public meetings virtually. The bill passed 66-4 in the Assembly and 28-7 in the Senate. The Piedmont City Council determined on Monday by a 5-0 vote that meeting in person presents imminent risks to the health and safety of attendees. Piedmont City Council met in person for the first time for its regularly scheduled meeting on Monday, October 4. The public is not yet invited to attend in-person, but may still participate virtually.

articles.text: What does the Bible say? One answer is: absolutely nothing. Maybe it’s the politics in the air and perhaps even in our drinking water, but whatever the source, it seems like there is a renewed desire to be on God’s side. The introductory phrase “the Bible says…” is back with a vengeance. But I can assure you that any sentence that begins with those words makes no sense whatsoever. That babbling Bible has told women to sit down and shut up, called science a tool of the devil and fueled anti-Semitism and racism. This theological ventriloquism has led people through valleys of guilt, shame and fear, no doubt to support the status quo and keep the powerful in power. This arrogant preface is defended with the argument that a true believer takes the word of God literally. But which word are we talking about? If we are talking about the actual words composed by the original authors of the books of the Bible then shouldn’t those who feel so strongly about the literal word only quote from the original language? Obviously the first thing to note is that the Bible is a translation in progress. For example, the Greek word for “sin” is the same word used in archery to describe an arrow that has simply missed its mark. In the original language the sense is that one might be just a little off from center and yet in many circles “sin” has come to be understood as a dark and gruesome plague that compels us to feel guilt, shame and self-loathing.
articles.title: Interpreting the Bible is hard work...and necessary

articles.text: Piedmont holds the distinction of being the most vaccinated city in Alameda County with over 90% of its eligible residents vaccinated. Residents are not immune, however, to “breakthrough” cases of COVID despite the high vaccination status among residents. According to the Center for Disease Control, vaccine “breakthrough” cases are expected, but rare. While vaccines are an “effective and critical tool to bring the pandemic under control…no vaccine is 100% effective at preventing illness,” the agency said. There is evidence that vaccination makes illness less severe, and that risk of infection, hospitalization, and death are all much lower in vaccinated people compared to unvaccinated. This was reiterated by Dr. George Rutherford, UCSF Epidiemiologist, at a League of Women Voters virtual forum in September. “Despite the fact that the vaccines work really well, we do have breakthrough cases where fully vaccinated people do get infected,” Dr. Rutherford said. “If you are unvaccinated you are 4.9 times more likely to be diagnosed with SARS-CoV-2, and 29.4 times more likely to be hospitalized [due to complications from the virus.]” Breakthrough cases On October 2, Piedmont Community Church issued an announcement alerting residents of a COVID incident. On September 28, church staff was informed that a volunteer who was in the Christian Education Building two days prior had tested positive for COVID-19. The person who was infected is fully vaccinated and was double-masked, Transitional Pastor Dr. Steve Schibsted said. “The individual was feeling fine on Sunday morning but started experiencing flu-like symptoms on Sunday evening. The individual was tested for COVID-19, received the test results on Tuesday and immediately informed Leslie Quantz, our Director of Children’s Ministries,” Dr. Schibsted said. The church then notified all people who were in contact with the individual, and those involved notified the Alameda County Public Health Department. County Health Department guidance The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) orders that all persons who are diagnosed with COVID-19 self-isolate for at least 10 days from their last exposure. This applies to both vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. “A close contact [exposure] is still defined as having spent 15 minutes within six feet of someone known to have COVID-19, either after they were diagnosed or up to two days before they started showing symptoms, or if you have had multiple brief exposures adding up to 15 minutes, especially if indoors, and even if you wore face coverings or masks,” said ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram. A person who is vaccinated and has been exposed does not need to quarantine if they don’t have symptoms, Balram added, but they are recommended to test for the virus three to five days after exposure. The County provided the following example: “if Alex received her second dose of the Moderna vaccine on January 1, and had close contact on March 31 with someone who later tested positive for COVID-19, Alex does not need to quarantine. However, she should continue to monitor for symptoms of infection until April 12. If she does develop symptoms during that time, she should immediately go into isolation and contact her health care provider.”

articles.text: The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) and state officials released its latest report of statewide COVID-19 data on October 1. As of October 1, California has 4,496,717 confirmed cases to-date. The seven-day positivity rate is 2.8%. The vast majority of confirmed cases are among the age group 18-49, with 2,564,360 of cases occurring in that age range. To date, there have been 68,796 COVID-related fatalities in the state, according to the CDPH. The average case rate among unvaccinated Californians age 16 or older is 57 per 100,000 per day, and the average case rate among vaccinated Californians is significantly lower at 7 per 100,000 for the week of September 19 through 25. Cases are occurring largely among unvaccinated populations, according to the CDPH. The rate among the unvaccinated is eight times the rate among vaccinated individuals. As of October 1, according to the Centers for Disease Control, 84% of eligible Californians have received at least one dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. Medical providers reported to CDPH that a total of 49,486,002 vaccine doses have been administered statewide. In Piedmont, the number of residents who are considered fully vaccinated is now slightly over 90%, according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Piedmont has had 267 COVID cases reported to-date.

articles.text: The Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Advisory Committee (PBAC) will hold a meeting tomorrow, October 7, to present the revised Piedmont Safer Streets plan. The public comment for the first draft of the Safer Streets Plan took place in July and August; during that period, the city received 46 emails and one phone call with comments from the public. The plan project team gave consideration to all comments and a revised initial draft plan incorporates them where appropriate. Comments are listed in the Safer Streets draft plan and were edited to remove personal-identification information. One respondent suggested “greater police effort to both stop and cite blatant stop sign violations by bicyclists.” Another respondent cited interest in “continuing to explore more ways to calm traffic in Wildwood from Grand Avenue to Nova.” Many comments were geared toward cycling routes and bicycle lanes, with suggestions for improvement or upgrades. “I must say I am disappointed in the solutions presented to address bicycle safety,” one respondent commented. “Road diets are good, and better than nothing. However, a skinny strip of white paint on the ground that is somehow supposed to keep cars away from bicycles, in reality do almost nothing.” The Piedmont Bicycle and Safety Advisory Committee held its first meeting a year ago, October 13, 2020, and is tasked with implementing a safe streets master plan. The plan builds on other local planning efforts, particularly the city’s general plan, the American with Disabilities Act Right-of-Way Transition Plan, Climate Action Plan, and Complete Streets policy. Enhanced street crossings are considered a high-priority project for the committee. The meeting will be held virtually tomorrow, October 7, at 5:30 p.m. For questions about the Piedmont Safer Streets project or about the committee, contact Gopika Nair, acting staff liaison for the committee, at (510) 420- 3054, or by email at saferstreets@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Public Works Department is working on the final design of a proposed pedestrian safety project at the corner of Oakland and El Cerrito avenues. The intersection was identified as a prominent pedestrian crossing for school children and was considered high-priority for pedestrian safety upgrades in the 2014 Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan and the 2021 Piedmont Safer Streets Plan. Currently a hand-operated flashing light exists at El Cerrito Avenue. In December 2018, City Council approved a contract with Coastland Engineers to design permanent bulb-outs and more safety improvements. Preliminary designs were considered at an April 2019 meeting, which included shortened crossing distances, high-visibility crosswalks, pedestrian ramps, refreshed painting and new signage. These designs allow for the installation of landscaping. Since 2014, minor improvements such as painted crosswalks and stop signs have been made at numerous intersections identified as high-priority. The Public Works Department recommended moving forward with the project due to its high-priority status. The cost of improvements at El Cerrito and Oakland Ave., and Jerome and Oakland Ave., one block west, is estimated at $400,000. The city council will review a more detailed engineer’s estimate. The city was awarded a $19,000 Safe Route to Schools mini-grant for the design phase of this project. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation has indicated its interest in raising funds for the project with its holiday 2021 campaign, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said. articles.text: Piedmont students in grades 3-12 filled out a survey on social and emotional health between August 23 and September 3 after the school district returned to full-time in-person learning. The survey, a Behavioral and Emotional Screening System, indicated an improvement of student wellbeing compared with a similar survey in March. The survey results were presented at the September 22 school board meeting, in an effort by the district to make student mental health a priority after the disruption of a year and a half due to COVID-19. The survey specifically targets emotional disabilities, leadership, social skills, and study skills. Externalizing and internalizing behaviors were also screened for, as were aggression, anxiety, and depression. “ Unt i l eve r yone fe els grounded and safe and included, real learning can’t happen, because you are distracted by all the other stuff. What we really want is to develop students with a lifetime of intellectual curiosity and we need to build the space to make that happen,” said board member Amal Smith. District-wide results showed that 1,592 or 86% of students in grades 3-12 who completed the survey, were at “normal risk” and were “adjusted and doing very well,” according to Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak. The school district administered the first survey in the spring of 2020, the second iteration in March this year, and now a third assessment. The student self-assessment form is administered online, has 28 items and takes about 15 minutes to complete. Survey results from March 2021, after 12 months of distance learning, showed 81% of students were at “normal risk” for social-emotional health issues, 13% at “elevated risk,” and 5% at “extremely elevated risk.” The most recent survey from the start of this school year shows that the “elevated risk” category has decreased from 250 to 210 students since March. The number of students classified in the category of “extremely elevated risk” has dropped from 99 to 59. On subscales, female students were more likely to fall into higher risk categories with only 82% of females in the lowest risk category versus 89% of males. Risk also increased steadily with age from 3rd grade to 9th grade. In the group of least concern, 3rd graders had 91%, 88% of 5th graders, 84% of 8th graders, and 80% of 9th graders. The trend does not continue for the rest of high schoolers with 85% of 10th graders, 82% of 11th graders and 86% of 12th graders in the least concerning category. In a message to faculty members, High School Principal Adam Littlefield noted, “We need to know our students’ faces and stories.” To watch the survey presentation to the school board, skip ahead 15 minutes on the September 22, school board meeting at (Piedmont.granicus.com/ MediaPlayer.php?view_id=3&- clip_id=2411).

School is back in session, and everyone is learning their math, science, language arts skills, and hopefully some play. My favorite part of school has always been story time. This activity happens in the classroom at all age levels, from circle time for the littles all the way to socratic seminars for the bigs. Storytelling is important from the very beginning of life. There is much research stating that storytelling is key for the developing brain, including creativity, imagination, vocabulary and communication. This early exposure to letters, words, and structure help children to read and write. Almost more importantly, storytelling and sharing aids children in telling their own stories allowing them to process and understand their own experiences, often reflecting their culture, language and history, contributing to the formation of identity. At Fairyland, I watch children enjoying the stories being told at the puppet theatre. So much is manifesting in a short 15-minute show - the recognition of a story with characters, values, emotions, and drama. This is evidenced by laughter, clapping, gasps and questions. As they build language and communication, stories also spark curiosity and engage us in realities other than our own. This trip into another reality gives us valuable perspective on our own experiences. What can you do to support storytelling with your little people? • Talk a lot. For babies and toddlers, narrate what you are doing or what you will be doing and integrate voice inflection to help the story flow. • • • Share who you are. Tell family histories or stories illustrating who you are as a unit. Write it down. Take dictation from your young storyteller and read it back to them. It often grows or gets clarified. Act it out. Help young storytellers dramatize the stories they tell by adding movement. Although the structured environment of language arts in the classroom is crucial, storytelling outside of the classroom is also important. Storytelling directly impacts the development of our children, and the effects have a powerful impact on our community. articles.text: There are many volunteer opportunities for high school and middle school students in the East Bay that fit around a traditional school schedule. Here are just a few. There are various ways you can volunteer with the organization, which is seeking volunteers to conduct mock interviews, style clients, facilitate workshops, and process donations. Wardrobe for Opportunity also accepts gently-used and new clothing donations. You can register for a self-guided cleanup by visiting Easy Bay Regional Park District (EBRPD) website at https://www.ebparks.org/about/getinvolved/ volunteer/events.htm. articles.text: Walk for Wellness 2021, the PUSD Wellness Center’s largest fundraiser of the year, attracted over 400 entrants who walked more than 1,700 miles collectively and raised more than $50,000 for the Wellness Center. The event was organized by the Wellness Center Support Committee, a group of parent volunteers committed to fundraising on behalf of the Wellness Center. “We’re thrilled with the success of Walk for Wellness,” said event co-chair KeriAnne Hohener. “All aspects of the event— the number of participants, the miles logged, the money raised — exceeded our expectations.” Walk for Wellness 2021 was an inclusive, accessible and fun event open to the entire Piedmont community. Participants received access to seven maps detailing various walks around town and picked up a bag of goodies - including a Walk for Wellness visor, mask, Clif bars, Ocho chocolates and coconut water from Harmless Harvest - at the Harvest Festival on Sunday, September 19. Fruit donated by Mulberry’s Market and Village Market was also included. During the week of September 20 walkers and runners logged mileage from their walks online, shared their favorite walks with other participants, and posted photos on social media. Piedmont High School parent Cindy Lee Gong logged an amazing 90.7 miles, followed closely by last year’s frontrunner Maria Carson Breber with 82.6 miles. Four additional walkers logged over 50 miles each: Jon Malan (78.2), Amber Brumfiel (60), Teebie Saunders (53.49) and Lisa Lomenzo (51.73). Everyone was thankful for an excuse to spend time outside for a good cause. Beach parent Jason Lee said his children Roland and Mia loved participating. “The kids really enjoyed the historical walk and had fun imagining the old buildings and sites as they were a hundred plus years ago,” Lee said. Dr. Alisa Crovetti, the Clinical Supervisor of the Wellness Center, is grateful that the Piedmont community understands the need for counseling services at the secondary school level. “It is absolutely crucial that Beach students Stella and Juliet Bindernagel enjoyed their outdoor walks with mom Emily Harrold. we prioritize the mental health of our students, especially during a global pandemic,” Dr. Crovetti said. “I’m thrilled with the response to Walk for Wellness and very much appreciate the community’s support of the Wellness Center.” The Wellness Center Support Committee is already thinking about Walk for Wellness 2022. “The enthusiasm for this year’s event was incredible. I think it is safe to say Walk for Wellness has become an annual event for the Piedmont community,” said event co-chair Nicki Gilbert. The Walk for Wellness Committee is grateful to the more than 40 Piedmont families who sponsored the event, and to the following corporate and in-kind sponsors: Ace Hardware, Anian & Adrienne, Bay Design & Build, Berkeley Orinda Orthodontics, Clif Bar, The Cooper Group, East Bay Pediatrics, The Grubb Co., Hillside View Orthodontics, Maggie and Dixie Lu insisted on accompanying owner and PHS parent Andrew Drake on all his walks. historical sites of Piedmont.

articles.text: Seventh grade students were thrilled to participate in the Medieval Banquet this year after a pause due to COVID. To start off the Banquet, a trumpet fanfare played and was heard by all on the patio. Students then performed the Maypole dance, prancing around the pole weaving ribbons, while flower girls threw petals into the crowd; then a lovely song-skit was performed. After, students moved into the Multi-Purpose Room, and the elaborately-costumed student King and Queen were introduced, followed by the lords and ladies of each Manor House. The Manor Houses were named after the seventh grade teachers. Next, a comedic skit was performed called “Erasmus Rules.” The students heard a thorough recitation of the banquet rules including, “Don’t stick your bare hands into the serving pot,” “Toss your bones on the floor,” and “Don’t pick your nose.” There were also many helpful public service announcements about how to avoid the plague and commercials for such services as “Lords and Ladies Marriage Counseling,” and various elixirs. Next was the Medieval “Circle Dance,” a very elegant dance with bows and curtsies. The banquet performances finished off strong with the “Pirate Stick Dance,” an incredibly impressive stick tapping routine with dramatic medieval music.
articles.title: Annual event through the eyes and in the words of students in Ted Scherman’s class

articles.text: From fancy to simple, extravagant to unembellished, costumes were a big part of the Medieval Banquet. There were a variety of costumes, as students were given a choice of their attire. The outfits brought us back to another time. Even though we were at a middle school in the 21st century, we were surrounded by people who made you feel like you were in the middle ages. Peasants roamed the school, with lords and ladies. Doctors adorned the infamous black plague mask, and jesters were in festive wear with monks and clergy. “It was fun seeing everyone’s creative and intuitive ideas,” said seventh grader Claire Aubrecht. “The costumes were beautiful, and brought the medieval banquet to life.”
articles.title: Elaborate costumes were everywhere

articles.text: After attending the Medieval Banquet in the MPR, students were invited outside to enjoy cookies and juice along with many fun activities including sword fighting, a medieval marriage, fortune telling, eat-the-donut-off-the-string, and Diet of Worms. The most popular among these was a game called Soak the Bloke in which students stand 10 yards away from a teacher held in imitation wooden stock (a form of medieval punishment). Students would throw wet sponges at the teachers to the cheers from the audience. A hearty crowd occupied half of the court, as students watched their classmates repeatedly drench their favorite teachers. When all the teachers participating had cycled through, students ran to take their places in the quickly filling up line of kids waiting for their turn to get soaked.
articles.title: Soak the Bloke

articles.text: When all the festivities were finished, students were beckoned to a court to perform the Electric Slide, dubbed the “Medieval Slide” to fit the theme. After weeks of practicing as a class, kids finally had a chance to dance together as an entire grade. With the song “Golden Years” by David Bowie playing, with inspiration from the movie A Knight’s Tale, students were in sync with one another as the graduating class of 2027. “It was a really fun way to connect with other students, especially after last year,” said 7th grader Elsa Wallway. A unifying event and opportunity to all stand (or rather, dance) together, everyone can agree that the Medieval Slide was truly unforgettable.

Piedmont had a clean 7-0 sweep of the Encinal Jets on Thursday, September 30 at a match played in Alameda. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 11-7 with six matches remaining before the WACC Championship Tournament on November 5-6. “We shut out Encinal on Thursday; they were forced to default at #4 singles and #3 doubles due to lack of players,” explained coach Jim Landes. “Everyone won in straight sets. It was another solid league win.” Bridgette McEfee, featured at No. 1 singles, won 6-2, 6-0, and sophomore Anika Gilliland won in straight sets at No. 2, 6-3, 6-3. Gilliland, a varsity starter for the first year, has won her last four matches, showing an ability to land forehands and manage the tempo of matches with wellplaced lobs. “I thought Anika played against a very good opponent. She mixed up her shots, as she usually does, with hard forehands, drop shots, and lobs. She has been playing better as the season has gone on,” said Landes. Rose Siemers, typically a doubles player, won easily, 6-2, 6-1, at No. 3 singles. “Rose also played very well, hitting with powerful groundstrokes for clean winners,” said Landes. Anika Gilliland won at No. 2 singles 6-3, 6-3. Cecilia Defazio and Emma Eisemon (not pictured) won their fourth match at No. 1 doubles, 6-2, 6-4.

articles.text: Piedmont’s football woes continued last Friday, October 1, with a 33-14 loss to the Washington of Fremont in a game before a home field crowd at Witter Field. Despite the score, the undermanned Highlanders were able to keep the game close at 13-6 in the third quarter. With only 17 players in uniform ad some injuries setting in, the Huskies powered through 20 points in the final 16 minutes. “Every week, we take a step forward and a couple of steps backwards. We had many opportunities, some dropped balls where we could’ve scored and penalties that pushed us back. We’re a young team and we’re building character. We have to take it a week at a time,” said coach Jerome Johnson. It was a strong day for receiver Evan McConathy with over 100 yards and two touchdowns. He now has four touchdowns this season. “I love Evan. He plays with heart, Said Johnson. “He’s a vital part of this team on both sides of the ball, and is a leader for us. It’s difficult to ask these guys to play all the positions we’re asking of them. Washington opened by intercepting a pass on the game’s second play at Piedmont’s 27-yard line. On a 7-play drive, the Huskies scored with 7:12 left in the quarter on a one-yard punch across the goal line on a 4th-and-1. Sophomore Dmitri Papahadjopoulos, a JV callup, leaped high to block the extra point attempt, to keep the score at 6-0. Papahadjopoulos and Emmett Maxwell were recently promoted from the junior varsity team. “Dmitri is a sophomore and is an upcoming kid. He has the potential to be a star for us; he’s just getting his feet wet and get the flow of playing varsity. It’s the same with Emmett, he’s a smart kid who can continue to learn the offense. He’s aggressive,” said Johnson. Piedmont countered by driving to the Washington 19-yard line, but failed to convert on a 4th-and-9. articles.text: In a defensive battle, Piedmont’s girls’ water polo team took a narrow 4-2 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, September 28 at the Laney College Pool. The Dragons scored first, with a goal with 1:37 remaining in the first quarter. Macie Gard scored for Piedmont 41 seconds before halftime with an assist from Odessa Dando. With a 1-1- tie, the defensive battle continued. Suddenly the Dragons came to life and scored two quick goals with 38 and 6 seconds left in the half to take a 3-1 lead. In the third quarter, the Dragons were able to score again after drawing an exclusion with 2:52 left in the quarter. Piedmont had chances to score, but the BOD goalie stopped shots from Rosie Feldman, Gard, and Frankie Broening. In the final quarter, Piedmont’s Dando got on the board with 2:35 minutes left to narrow the score to 4-2, but couldn’t score again. Dando finished with a goal and assist, and Gard had one goal. articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 3-0 loss to Alameda on Thursday, September 30 at Binks Rawlings Gym. Despite the straight-set victory for the Hornets, all three games were close, with scores of 25-23, 25-21, 27-25. “It’s frustrating, but it also feels good that we’re right there on the cusp of success,” said PHS coach Leslie Blakely. “We were in the game. There are things we need to work on, but I’m proud. I don’t like losing, but Alameda is a good school. We competed well tonight.” Piedmont led in all of the games, but was unable to put together a final string of points to ensure victory. “I think we played well. They are a good team; it’s important for us to play teams like Alameda because we try to match them and take it as a challenge. I’m proud of how we worked tonight,” added senior leader Ruby Shaffer. “We played as a team,” added outside hitter Tara Kothari, a junior. “Going forward, we know we have to keep our heads in it on those critical points. It’s just getting past that one-point difference; that’s really been our Achilles heel lately.” “We have a saying: ‘finish the point,’” stated sophomore Brie DeYoung. “We’ve shown we can get that done.” Brie DeYoung (left) and Sadie Towns go up for a block. Sadie Towns had six kills and two aces against the Hornets. Match Recap In the first game, the two sides traded points with Piedmont consistently holding a 1-2 point lead until the score reached 22-20 in favor of the Highlanders. Alameda scored three straight points to go ahead 23-22. Shaffer tied it at 23-23 with a hard spike, but two straight kills by Hornets’ Drew Bryant gave them the win, 25-23. In Game 2, PHS again opened with a lead, 3-0, then 7-3 before the Hornets scored nine points to take the lead, 12-8. The Highlanders rallied to once again hold a lead, 18-15 and held a 20-19 advantage before the match was tied at 21-21. The Hornets went ahead 22-21, and Bryant slammed down three straight kills to win it for Alameda, 25-21. The third game was even closer and went into overtime before Alameda pulled out a victory at 27-25. In a battle from the beginning, the two sides exchanged points until PHS held a 19-14 lead and appeared to be in control. But the Hornets rallied for five straight points to pull even at 19-19. Alameda inched ahead, 21-20, only to see Piedmont rally once more for a 23-21 lead on an Alameda service error and a serving ace by Sadie Towns. Tied at 23-23, Shaffer recorded a block to put Piedmont up 24-23, but Alameda responded with a block of its own. The Hornets then committed an offensive error to put PHS up 25-24, holding set point. But then Alameda’s Bryant and Michelle Ganbaatar recorded consecutive kills, for a 26-25 lead, and won the match with a serving ace. Final stats include Shaffer with five kills, two aces and two blocks. Sadie Towns had six kills and two aces. Kothari had two kills and an ace. DeYoung had two kills and two blocks. Shelby Cavenaugh had three kills and a block. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-5) hosts San Leandro on Thursday, October 7 at 6:30 p.m. The team will compete in the 13th annual Stockton Classic on Saturday, October 9.

articles.text: A group exhibition showcasing a selection of artworks by eight female artists from the East Bay opened last weekend at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit, titled 8WA, will be on view Saturdays and Sundays through October 24 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. or by appointment. The exhibition features the work of Laura Abrams, Deborah Green, Michelle Lewis, Laura McNall, Juliet Mevi, Jacqui Rubenstein, Ariella Seidenberg, and Caskey Weston. Nearly 70 works are on display. “We appreciate this opportunity to present a self-curated show from our personal collections,“ said Deborah Green, the artist who initiated the project. “I am proud to be part of this group of so many talented and accomplished women, and we Sacred Loons, by Michelle Lewis, 16 x 16 Life Blooms in My Garden, by Ariella Seidenberg, 11 x 14 are looking forward to exhibiting a strong body of artwork in this beautiful space. It’s especially meaningful to be emerging with a collective show after months of pandemic isolation. Works on display showcase a wide variety of styles and media. Growing out of an association through the Northern California Women’s Caucus for Art, many of the artists here embrace its activist mission with works that put forward dynamic feminist, environmental, and social justice messages.” Gallery hours are free and open to the public, and no reservation is required. For more information, email paintpeace@ yahoo.com, or visit www.piedmontcenterforthearts.org.
articles.title: Eight Women Artists exhibit now at Center for the Arts

articles.text: Shotgun Players will perform The Claim for both in-person and online streaming. Live performances will take place at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley October 14 through October 30, and livestream performances are available October 21 and 28. The Claim, written by Tim Crowbury and directed by Rebecca Novick, explores the ways in which individuals seek asylum in the United Kingdom. The production is part of Shotgun Players’ Bridge Programming, a series of productions designed to transition the company back to live performances. In-person capacity for the show will be capped at 75%. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse will produce Michael Gene Sullivan’s play, The Great Khan, live October 13 through November 13. The show is directed by Darryl Jones and will be streamed live November 13. The play follows protagonist Jayden, an African American teenager who saves a girl, Ant, from sexual assault. Following the incident, Jayden and his mother are forced to move to keep him safe from the boys who attacked Ant. Both Ant and Jayden try to figure out how to define themselves in a culture that insists on seeing them as forever dangerous. This is part of a rolling world premiere of a production that is part of the National New Play Network. Tickets are available now. A seating chart with fixed social distancing will be used, and masks will be required during the performance. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is also required to attend the performance. To purchase tickets, visit www.sfplayhouse.org. San Francisco Playhouse will produce The Great Khan beginning October 13.
articles.title: The Great Khan opens at SF Playhouse October 13

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, will present an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum of Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition will be on display from October 20 through February 27. “Soul of Black Folks” is the premier museum solo exhibition for Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo and is a presentation of over 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artist’s paintings that actively center Black subjectivity anchored by extremely calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working in Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. The text by sociologist W.E.B Du Bois inspires the Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo’s solo show opens October 20 at the Museum of African Diaspora on Mission Street in San Francisco. exhibition title which aims to be a study of “Black life behind the veil of race.” To learn more about the upcoming exhibition, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibition/ amoako-boafo-soul-of-blackfolks/. The museum is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco.

articles.text: Trumpeter, singer and songwriter Bria Skonberg will perform a concert at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on October 9, as part of Cal Performances 2021-22 season. Skonberg’s most recent release, “Nothing Never Happens,” includes arrangements of music by Queen, the Beatles, Duke Ellington, and others. She made her Cal Performances debut last winter through the organization’s digital platform, and now returns for a live concert on October 9 accompanied by her jazz band. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony opener under new maestro EsaPekka Salonen was novel, modern, and unique, certainly unlike any in over half a century of this writer’s memory and attendance. He featured rousing and in part explosive music, none of it familiar, all from 1939 or later. And the performance earned several standing ovations. The patrons’ enthusiasm over the unencumbered reopening of Louise Davies Hall after a year and a half was palpable. Some spoil-sports will grouse about the lack of National Anthem, the flag, and beloved old Americana favorites. Others will bristle at the glitzy 500-plus dancing lights on stage, perhaps a throwback to the Finn’s former Los Angeles tenure. But folks: Give him some slack! Salonen threw down the gauntlet in his first indoor S.F. opening night to start his second season: No totally predictable, businessas-usual symphony programs, but rather diversity, mind-stretching, and visceral stimuli. The audience went along, quite unpredictably, with vim and vigor, responding to a live on-stage ballet, a lengthy jazz piece with solo vocalist, an Adams modernism, a notable Latino component, and a dozen percussionists running wild. And for once there was no mad dash at the last cadence to rush to the after-party and “nosh pit” eateries in Lake Louise. And, significantly, the audience for the gala had shifted, on average a good two decades younger Soprano Esperanza Spalding also performed with San Francisco Symphony on contrabass. than in past years, with greater participation by the black community, drawn in part by a Black choreographer (Alonzo King) and composer (Wayne Shorter). The initial reaction suggested that conductor-composer Salonen was an adroit choice to succeed the retired MTT (still out of action on sick leave) in being bold and innovative, selecting dissimilar vectors to MTT’s. If the hall’s roof was blown off, credit the nimble dozen SFS percussionists playing up a storm in Silvestre Revueltas’ 1939 “Night of Enchantment” excerpt. Somewhat influenced by Stravinsky’s unbridled “Rite of Spring,” it was an 11-minute virtuoso tour, supplemented by a wind player blowing on a conch shell. Revueltas falls into a group of creative composers felled in mid-career, alongside Bizet, Schubert, Mozart, and Mendelssohn. Star power came from the lower-case, but ever-high-quality esperanza spalding, a bone fide double threat on contrabass

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony, led by Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen and featuring flutist Claire Chase and pianist Jeremy Denk, will perform a series of concerts entitled “Exotic Birds” being performed October 14 through 17. The magic of the natural world is at the heart of this program, bookended by Claude Debussy’s Prelude a l’pares-midi d’un faune and La Mer. Two works inspired by the majesty of birds and avian wildlife incorporate pianist Denk and flutist Chase. Denk will perform Olivier Messianen’s Oiseaux Exotiques, incorporating the songs of 47 bird species, and Chase, a San Francisco Symphony Collaborative Partner, will perform Kaija Saariaho’s Aile du songe (Winged Dream). Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen leads the San Francisco Symphony in a series of performances entitled “Exotic Birds.” All performances will be in-person at Davies Symphony Hall. Performances Thursday through Saturday will begin at 7:30 p.m., and the final Sunday performance will begin at 2 p.m. Tickets may be purchased by visiting https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2021-22/EXOTIC-BIRDS.

articles.text: Fidelio, originally titled Leonore, is Beethoven’s only opera. The libretto tells the story of Leonore, disguised as a prison guard named “Fidelio,” rescues her husband Florestan from a political prison. The opera combines the themes of personal sacrifice, heroism, and triumph with Beethoven’s own political outlook. The performance by San Francisco Opera is a modern-day ref lection of incarceration. Directed by Matthew Ozawa, this new production of Fidelio stard Elza van den Heever, Russell Thomas and Greer Grimsley. Music Director Eun Sun Kim conducts the triumphant score, which is a precursor to Beethoven’s later work, Symphony No. 9. The opera is sung in German with English supertitles. The opera will be performed for two weeks, through October 30. For tickets, visit https:// sfopera.com/on-stage/fidelio/. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré In a recent New Yorker article by Agnes Callard, titled The Problem of Marital Loneliness, she writes, “Marriage is hard, even when no crises loom, and even when things basically work. What makes it hard are not the various problems that arise but the lingering absence that is felt most strongly when they don’t. The very closeness of marriage makes every bit of distance palpable. Something is wrong all the time.” What Callard is writing about is the loneliness experienced in marriage, her referent being Ingmar Bergman’s Scenes From a Marriage, which debuted in Sweden in 1973, and has only recently been contemporized by Hagai Levi in five episodes, now streaming on HBO. The series stars two extraordinary actors: Jessica Chastain as Mira, a tightly wound tech executive, and Oscar Isaac as her husband, Jonathan, a philosophy professor and principal homemaker. They have a four-year-old daughter. The series opens with the couple being interviewed by a graduate student who is writing her thesis on the qualities inherent in those marriages that have lasted – in the case of Mira and Jonathan they’ve been married for 10 years. As a stand alone vignette, their answers are compelling, and at times painful to watch, often edged with their awkward but sincere efforts to affirm the other’s responses in a sensitive and accommodating way, while trying to mirror the essence of what the other is trying to say. Their first crisis, of sorts, takes place after the interview when Mira reveals to Jonathan that she is pregnant and they both explore how the other feels about the profound changes that having a second child will bring to their lives. Embedded in their interaction is the tentative question regarding how they will confront the decision should they decide not to keep the child and choose to have an abortion. There are long moments of hesitation, of reflection, of lucidity and tenderness. A second Oscar Isaac and Jessica Chastain star in the 5 part HBO miniseries, Scenes from a Marriage. child will deeply impact their personal and professional lives, and Mira acknowledges, with some guilt and regret, that Jonathan will of course shoulder most of the childcare responsibility. As they struggle to build a bridge across this moment, I was reminded of blind men trying to identify an elephant by touch. My faith in their ability to find a resolution, that reflects both their wishes, is steeped in uncertainty; they are together and yet they are apart. Having viewed episode three, it became clear that there is a far greater crisis confronting them than just the possible birth of a second child. It is one that crystalizes their individual loneliness in the marriage. After three episodes, I found myself awaiting the next installment. There is something, however, that Levi does at the beginning of each episode that surprised me and I wonder if it isn’t a creative miscalculation. He breaks the fourth wall, a performance convention that assumes there is a box around the staged scene/ actors with walls on three sides. The fourth wall is that imagined line, a chimera of sorts, which exists between the actors and the audience. The actors ignore the audience, existing in what Konstantin Stanislavski referred to as the “public solitude,” and behave as they would in private while knowing they are being observed. Levi opens each episode having the actors walk through the set, guided by Covid-masked assistants, directing them to the room where the scene will be shot. When asked about his breaking of the fourth wall – in effect looking straight into the camera, Levi says, “This is not about this very specific couple… it’s much more general, much more abstract…” Universal, perhaps? I feel it is an unnecessary conceit and only serves to lessen the powerful impact of the resonating drama that so intensely unfolds. Scenes From a Marriage. Written by Hagai Levi. Starring Jessica Chastain, Oscar Isaac, Nicole Beharrie. Five episodes now streaming on HBO.

articles.text: Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio star in Revolutionary Road. Review by Chris Honoré Revolutionary Road is a tour de force of acting. In fact, it’s an actors’ film from the first frame to the final credits. What carries the story forward is dialogue; the narrative is sustained almost entirely by the content and intensity of the characters’ interactions. Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio are remarkable as April and Frank Wheeler, a 1950’s couple who suddenly find they are living lives which no longer resemble those that they had so idealistically planned when they first met. Seven years after they were wed they become aware that they are living in a respectable house in suburban Connecticut, the parents of two children, while Frank commutes by train daily to New York City. He hates his job and April’s hopes of being an actress have been consumed on the pyre known as community theater. But instead of finding their way to one another, sharing their disappointments and truths, they begin to vent long simmering anger and grievances, at first with voices raised and then with a rage that knows no bounds, intended only to hurt. (No one, it seems, goes through life with just carry-on.) Sensing that they are in jeopardy, April insists that they leave everything behind and move to Paris in hopes of recapturing old dreams. “Let’s live life as it’s meant to be lived,” she offers. However seductive the plan seems, initially, there is a sense about it that is fragile and tentative. A dream that is unable to withstand the ever-present fact that they are too ensnared by their lives and commitments, all of which are the antithesis of revolution, give an ironic meaning to their address. The arc of this film does not lead to redemption. For April and Frank, there is no exit. They are unable to form an alliance and thus rescue themselves from the pervasive existential angst and ennui that grips them. It was Jean-Paul Sartre who said that “hell is other people.” And it was Henry David Thoreau who wrote, ”The mass of men live lives of quiet desperation and go to the grave with the song still in them.” What makes Revolutionary Road compelling is the ensemble of fine actors, to include an exceptional performance by Michael Shannon as an intensely perceptive wing-nut who visits the Wheelers with his mother and father. Surprisingly, his nomination for best supporting actor was the only serious nod the film received, despite its dark and haunting subject matter that has, in years past, enthralled the Academy. Revolutionary Road. Starring Kate Winslet, Leonardo DiCaprio, David Harbour, Kathyrn Hahn and Michael Shannon. Directed by Sam Mendes. Rated R.

articles.text: A scene from Disney’s James and the Giant Peach. The Disney animated feature James and the Giant Peach is based on the much-loved 1961 children’s book by Roald Dahl, and, like most well done movies intended for a young audience, it casts a spell, even when it’s a bit scary. But then kids like scary if served up with just the right amount of tart fairy tale fantasy. This story, both outlandish and humorous, introduces a British orphan, James (Paul Terry), who has lost his doting parents and now finds himself living on a mountain top with two sadistic aunts, Spiker and Sponge (Joanna Lumley, Miriam Margolyes). Cruelly, they have turned the youngster into a chore boy, callously ignoring the fact that he is their sympathetic nephew who is suffering due to his muchchanged circumstances. One day a strange old man appears (Pete Postlewaite) and gives a bag full of crocodile tongues to James, who accidentally drops them on the ground. As it happens, they fertilize a barren peach tree, which miraculously produces a giant peach. The peach offers James, now 7 years old, a kind of sanctuary. He discovers that inside the peach resides a menagerie of large garden bugs, some the size of James. There’s a brash centipede, an aristocratic British caterpillar, a sultry spider, a matronly ladybug, an old green grasshopper, a glowworm, and an earthworm. All anthropomorphic. Mr. Centipede, hearing the aunts searching for James, in a moment of protective panic, cuts the stem of the giant peach from the tree, sending it and its cohort rolling down the hill, knocking the aunts aside, coming to rest in the ocean. articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré There are multiple generations for whom the works of Roald Dahl are memorable. The Witches is one such story. First released in 1990 and then remade in 2020, this latest iteration blends state-of-the-art computer graphics and special effects with real life actors. Originally set in Britain, director Robert Zemeckis moved the tale to Alabama, principally to the Grand Orleans Imperial Hotel where an international coven of witches, led by the imperious Grand High Witch (Anne Hathaway), has gathered for a convention. The narrative opens with a young boy, Charlie Hansen (Jahzir Bruno), after having lost his parents in a car crash, goes to live with his grandmother (Octavia Spencer). To ease his loss, and hopefully cheer him up, she buys him a pet mouse that he names Daisy (Kristin Chenoweth). Wanting to build a small house for Daisy, Charlie and his grandmother go to a hardware store. While there, he is approached by a woman who tries to lure him away, but is interrupted by Charlie’s grandmother calling to him. He tells his grandmother about the strange encounter and she explains that the woman was a witch and that indeed witches do exist and once they find a child they never leave. His grandmother also tells Charlie how to identify a witch from an ordinary woman. Witches wear gloves to cover their claws, and wigs to disguise their baldness. They have square feet with no toes, their eyes have a purple tinge, and they possess a powerful sense of smell that they use to sniff out children. Worried, the two move to a nearby hotel, the Grand Orleans, but a hotel where the witches happen to be meeting. Also staying at the hotel is a boy named Bruno (Codie-Lei Erstick) who befriends Charlie. The two, along with Daisy the mouse, explore the hotel, entering the Grand Ballroom. They hear the witches coming and the three hide in a vent under the dais. There they overhear the Grand High Witch explain that she has invented a chocolate bar confection, one laced with a special potion that will turn children, who are despised, into mice. But Charlie and Bruno are discovered and turned into mice. They learn that Daisy was once a young girl. And so begins the adventure of Charlie, Daisy and Bruno who, along with the grandmother, are desperate to develop a plan to get a sample of the potion, hoping to be able to turn them back into children. This will involve a dinner of pea soup and a stolen potion served to the unsuspecting coven. Chaos, of course, ensues. Ann Hathaway’s performance is extraordinary. She is clearly enjoying portraying the petty, evil, vain Grand Witch. The feature’s voice-over is by Charlie, now grown up. The Witches is a Halloween treat and should delight kids age 8 and older. Keep in mind that this story can be scary-lite, and it does have more than a few creepy moments. The Witches. Directed by Robert Zemeckis. articles.text: Piedmont Seniors members celebrate the group’s 25th anniversary. Pictured are: (front) Greg Jurin (left), Yorkman Lowe, Mona Jamieson, Tanya Hu, Bev Becker, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Mary Finley, Janet Epstein; (back) Larry Hu, Carol Morrison, Elene Manolis, Irene Westler, Jeanne Gordon, Susan McCreary, Barbara Friede, Barbara Cox, Penny Robb, and Fred Pemberton. The Piedmont Seniors, sponsored since its inception by the Piedmont Recreation Department, celebrated its 25th Anniversary on Wednesday, September 22 at the Piedmont Community Center. They were treated to champagne and mimosas as well as homemade cookies to mark the occasion. Special recognition and gifts were given to individuals who had been with the group the longest. Barbara Cox, joined in January 1999, and Mona Jamieson joined the following year to “try something new”, she said. She was impressed by the sense of community she found as a recent widow, as well as the opportunity to learn about new things. Both members play an important part in the organization. Lois Dawers, a longtime Piedmont resident, along with Mark Delventhal, the former Recreation Director, formed the Piedmont Seniors as a way for people to remain socially active after the loss of a spouse. Lois felt there was a void in programs for active seniors, and Mark agreed. They both recognized the importance of socializing and friendship as keys to successful aging. One of the goals of the Piedmont Seniors is to provide a relaxed place to meet other seniors in an informal atmosphere. A major goal is to strengthen the social and emotional well-being of seniors, in addition to promoting the pursuit of intellectual development through participating in Bay Area excursions, speakers and special events. Although the monthly gatherings usually end around noon, those who remain continue to do fun things like watching a pre-selected movie or playing board games. The culmination of each year’s activities is a festive luncheon with music in December, usually held at the Claremont Country Club or the Bellevue Club. The members were recently introduced to Piedmont’s new Fire Chief, Dave Brannigan, as well as the new Recreation Department supervisor, Eva Phalen. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers and Lisa Douglas, Support Services Supervisor at the Police Department, have been speakers several times in the past and given tips to help seniors stay safe. Guest speakers talk about a myriad of subjects of special interest to seniors. Past speakers have represented Legal Assistance for Seniors, CHP Driving class specially tailored for senior drivers, balance classes, California Telephone Access for seniors with hearing or visual impairments, and Rotary International. To date the group has gone on nearly 250 excursions throughout the Greater Bay Area. Some past excursions include the Canine Companions for Independence in Santa Rosa, the Buck Institute on Aging in Novato, Filoli Gardens in Woodside. Rosie the Riveter National Historical Park in Richmond, the Hiller Aviation Museum in San Carlos, and the various museums in and around the Bay Area, along with exciting local musical theatre. “It is wonderful to finally re-open after 16 months of relative isolation due to Covid-19 protocol,” said Janet Epstein, the Piedmont Seniors Coordinator. “Extensive research has found that social isolation is as dangerous as smoking 2-3 packs of cigarettes a day!”. Janet has been with the group since its inception in 1996. The Seniors are community minded. Each year they generously contribute to the annual Toys for Tots program sponsored by the Piedmont Fire Department. They are always the first to fill toy barrels furnished by the Piedmont Fire Department. They have been involved in the nationwide “Socks for Seniors” project benefiting low-income seniors in nursing homes in the East Bay. They have donated dozens of socks and sundries over the years and have been touched by the appreciation of the underserved members of the local community. The Piedmont Seniors group meets on the 4th Wednesday of the month at the Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, from 10 a.m. to noon for refreshments and socializing. Piedmont residency is not a requirement to join. The group always welcomes new members. She helps people translate their personal experiences into stories on the page. Her topic is “ Everyone has a story-- What’s Yours” Wednesday, November 24 – Jean Goldman, a professional move organizer, will discuss the topic “Your kids don’t want your stuff”. articles.text: Technically zucchini is a fruit since it grows from the flower of a plant and contains the seeds for the plant (a vegetable is every other part of the plant). Most of us use zucchini as a vegetable, but with my sweet tooth, I will take any opportunity to bake up a dessert with what is at hand. I had planned to prepare a squash or pumpkin cake, but then realized I had purchased too many zucchinis on successive market days. Fortunately, in our climate, we will still see zucchini at our farmers markets for weeks to come. This recipe only uses two small-to-medium zukes, so you may have enough on hand now to try this satisfying cake. Feel free to switch up or add spices to the cinnamon. Hint: A bit of cardamom adds a bright note to the cake. PREPARATION Crumb topping: Mix together all the ingredients except the walnuts. You could do this either manually (using a fork or a pastry blender) or pulse it in a food processor. Stir in the nuts. Set aside until needed, in the refrigerator if your kitchen is warm. Cake: Zucchini Crumb Cake Adapted from: Baking from My Home to Yours Yield: One 9-inch round cake INGREDIENTS Crumb topping: 5 tablespoons unsalted butter, cold 2 tablespoons sugar 1/4 cup light brown sugar 1/ 2 cup flour 1/ 2 teaspoon cinnamon 1/ 8 teaspoon salt 1/ 2 cup walnuts, coarsely chopped For the cake: 1-1/ 2 cup zucchini, grated on the larger shred size 2 cups all-purpose flour 2 teaspoons baking powder 1/ 2 teaspoon baking soda 1/ 4 teaspoon salt 1/ 2 teaspoon cinnamon, ground 1/ 2 cup sugar 1/ 2 cup butter, plus 1 tablespoon for the pan 2 large eggs 1-1/ 2 teaspoon vanilla extract 1/ 2 cup heavy cream 1 teaspoon lemon juice 1. Preheat the oven to 350°F/175°C. Butter the sides of a 9-inch round pan and line the bottom with parchment paper. 2. Sift together the flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt and cinnamon. 3. Pour heavy cream into a small bowl and add the lemon juice. The mixture will curdle a bit, it’s OK. Set aside. 4. In a large bowl, beat the sugar and the butter with a hand mixer until light and airy – about three minutes. Add the vanilla. 5. Add the eggs one at a time, beating well after each to fully incorporate. 6. Add the shredded zucchini and mix to just incorporate. 7. Reduce the speed of the beater and add the flour in three parts and the cream in two parts alternately; starting and ending with flour. The batter will be fairly thick. 8. Transfer the batter in the buttered pan and even out the top with a spatula. 9. Sprinkle the crumb topping evenly over the batter, taking care to spread it out to the edges for full coverage and crumble tastiness in every bite. 10. Bake for about 50 minutes or until the crumbs are golden and a skewer comes out clean. articles.text: Piedmont resident Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. PP: What made you decide to start a site for education, counseling, and support for grandparents? CK: When I was an “expectant grandparent” I wondered whether having a grandchild would bear any resemblance to how I remembered new motherhood 30 years earlier. It turned out that it did – and then again, it didn’t. I found that there were very few resources I could turn to when looking for updated grandparenting guidance. I felt that my experience as a genetic counselor could be useful as I embarked on this journey to help other new grandparents. PP: What are some of the factors that influence the role grandparents will have in the family? CK: There are many important factors that can make a difference in how a grandparent may fit into a young family’s life. They include the grandparents’ ages and fitness, their geographic proximity to the grandchildren, how they have envisioned becoming a grandparent, whether they have a history of a positive, supportive relationship with their adult child and the child’s partner, and the memories/experiences of their own grandparents if they grew up with them. PP: What are the most common concerns that new grandparents ask? CK: Changes in pediatric recommendations for sleep, nutrition, safety, and discipline pose concerns for many grandparents. New parents have dozens of sources beyond basic baby books, and they consult them regularly to affirm that they are making good choices in raising their children. Grandparents have fewer resources and may not know which ones to trust. Other concerns include how to be an active part of their grandchildren’s lives whether they live close by or miles away. PP: How do conflicts tend to come up between grandparents and young parents? CK: Conflicts between young parents and grandparents grow less often out of real disrespect or malice, and more often out of difficulties in communication. Conflicts tend to arise in the same way that they arise in other areas of family life. The difference now is that the balance of decision-making power (choices being made for the children) resides with the young parent. For the older generation, this shift can be quite an adjustment. Grandparents can be left feeling that their experience and wisdom is not wanted or needed, while their caregiving and financial support continue to be requested. PP: Can you give an example of a concern that a grandparent has brought to you for guidance and advice? CK: The COVID-19 pandemic has presented many issues that have caused problems for families with grandchildren. Deep differences in how family members view risk can result in family discord. For example, young parents who are extremely cautious about their children being exposed to COVID-19 may clash dramatically with anti-vaccinator grandparents, and may disallow visitation unless the grandparents get vaccinated. Alternately, worried elders may feel that their children are exposing very young grandchildren to unnecessarily risky situations, and don’t feel listened to when they express their concerns. PP: In what ways do you believe that grandparent support groups can enhance a grandparent’s experience? CK: Grandparenthood happens when it happens. Many Cynthia Kane seniors have no friends who are yet grandparents or have friends whose grandchildren are much older. It can be hard to find an affinity group for new or new-ish grandparents. A grandparent support group allows grandparents to share their feelings and experiences in a safe, confidential environment. They can learn how other grandparents handled similar situations and find comfort in knowing that others feel as they do. PP: What are three key messages you can share with expectant or new grandparents? CK: 1) Ask how you can help. Instead of guessing, ask the new parents what you can do now and in the future to support them in their important new role as parent. 2) Keep the focus on the grandchild; don’t make the issue about you. If there is a disagreement, think about what is best for the grandchild and do that. 3) Be a role model: Be kind, brave, generous, forgiving, positive, and loving. Your child will be grateful and your grandchild will emulate you. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com.

They include the grandparents’ ages and fitness, their geographic proximity to the grandchildren, how they have envisioned becoming a grandparent, whether they have a history of a positive, supportive relationship with their adult child and the child’s partner, and the memories/experiences of their own grandparents if they grew up with them. PP: What are the most common concerns that new grandparents ask? CK: Changes in pediatric recommendations for sleep, nutrition, safety, and discipline pose concerns for many grandparents. New parents have dozens of sources beyond basic baby books, and they consult them regularly to affirm that they are making good choices in raising their children. Grandparents have fewer resources and may not know which ones to trust. Other concerns include how to be an active part of their grandchildren’s lives whether they live close by or miles away. PP: How do conflicts tend to come up between grandparents and young parents? CK: Conflicts between young parents and grandparents grow less often out of real disrespect or malice, and more often out of difficulties in communication. Conflicts tend to arise in the same way that they arise in other areas of family life. The difference now is that the balance of decision-making power (choices being made for the children) resides with the young parent. For the older generation, this shift can be quite an adjustment. Grandparents can be left feeling that their experience and wisdom is not wanted or needed, while their caregiving and financial support continue to be requested. PP: Can you give an example of a concern that a grandparent has brought to you for guidance and advice? CK: The COVID-19 pandemic has presented many issues that have caused problems for families with grandchildren. Deep differences in how family members view risk can result in family discord. For example, young parents who are extremely cautious about their children being exposed to COVID-19 may clash dramatically with anti-vaccinator grandparents, and may disallow visitation unless the grandparents get vaccinated. Alternately, worried elders may feel that their children are exposing very young grandchildren to unnecessarily risky situations, and don’t feel listened to when they express their concerns. PP: In what ways do you believe that grandparent support groups can enhance a grandparent’s experience? CK: Grandparenthood happens when it happens. Many Cynthia Kane seniors have no friends who are yet grandparents or have friends whose grandchildren are much older. It can be hard to find an affinity group for new or new-ish grandparents. A grandparent support group allows grandparents to share their feelings and experiences in a safe, confidential environment. They can learn how other grandparents handled similar situations and find comfort in knowing that others feel as they do. PP: What are three key messages you can share with expectant or new grandparents? CK: 1) Ask how you can help. Instead of guessing, ask the new parents what you can do now and in the future to support them in their important new role as parent. 2) Keep the focus on the grandchild; don’t make the issue about you. If there is a disagreement, think about what is best for the grandchild and do that. 3) Be a role model: Be kind, brave, generous, forgiving, positive, and loving. Your child will be grateful and your grandchild will emulate you. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group knew they were going to have a special walk on September 29, but no one could have guessed a record turnout of 50 people (and three K-9 best friends) might show up. The large gathering was due to the announcement that Hope Salzer had agreed to take them on a mini-tour of Piedmont Connect’s Healthy Landscapes Fall Front Garden Tour. Piedmont Connect is a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. Hope is its communications chair, and a member of the Healthy Landscapes team. A total of 14 gardens were part of this year’s Garden Tour, a nine-day event that offers a sampling of drought-tolerant and native-dominant landscaping showing the beauty of Piedmont in early fall. The tour features Piedmont front gardens that have been transformed from conventional water-intensive or invasive landscapes into creative, healthy landscapes of a variety of styles. The locations of the gardens are available at https://www. piedmontconnect.org/. Because of time and distance constraints, Wednesday’s plan was for Hope to take the walkers to five gardens in northwest Piedmont. The day started with Hope being introduced to the group and her description of how she became involved in Piedmont Connect and environmental sustainability. She made a heartfelt statement that today’s adult generations have not cared for our planet and environment as we should have. She feels what she, and we, are leaving our children is not what it should be. Because of this, Hope decided to learn about native species and what we can do to better protect our environment. Even more importantly, she is acting on and sharing this knowledge. The group continued to 310 Hillside where Hope told them of the owner’s involvement and commitment to making his garden environmentally strong, something that seemed to be the case with all the tour’s homeowners. Hope described the different plants in the garden and stressed the beauty of plants and flowers during all stages of their lifecycle, even as they fade and then decay. She said that the common practice of deadheading flowers may keep them from seeding and providing food for birds. The importance of butterflies, bees, and other insects in a healthy environment was also stressed. After Hope finished her comments, the group squeezed together on the driveway next door for a group photo. There were a lot of longtime regulars on the walk, but many first-time walkers, too. Hope recently registered for Walking on Wednesdays because she likes the exercise. The next garden destination was 10 Mesa Avenue. The large group walked up Oakland Avenue to Highland Avenue. Along Highland the group couldn’t resist noting the front garden of a home that is not on Piedmont Connect’s tour, but still has an impressive, natural landscape garden.
